                                          STAFF’S RESPONSE BRIEF


         SPS contends that accepting the arguments of Utility Division Staff in this docket would

 “derail the Signatories’ significant efforts to reach a Comprehensive Stipulation that, without

 question, is in the public interest.” 1 This is false. Staff not only questions the merits of the

 stipulation but has affirmatively demonstrated, through testimony and evidence, that this

 fundamentally flawed agreement is not, in fact, in the public interest. As explained below, contrary

 to the arguments of SPS and the Signatories, the $90 million increase in revenues is not reasonable

 and would result in unjust rates for New Mexico customers. Staff therefore respectfully submits

 this reply brief to urge the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission to uphold the public

 interest by rejecting the stipulation.

                                                 INTRODUCTION

            SPS and the Signatories emphasize the Stipulation’s broad support and the reduction from

  SPS’s original request. Those considerations may be relevant, but they do not substitute for the

  Commission’s independent obligation to determine whether the stipulated rates are just,

  reasonable, and lawful. 2 This is a Future-Test-Year rate case. Therefore, the Commission must

     determine whether the selected test period best reflects the conditions expected when rates take

     effect. 3 The record identifies specific material changes in resource adequacy assumptions, an

 unresolved ELI regulatory asset balance, and forecast based allocation issues that render the

 foundation on which this stipulation rests fundamentally unsound.


                                                   ARGUMENT

I.      The Stipulated $90 Million Revenue Requirement Is Based on Stale Data and Not
        Independently Supported
            In an application for increased rates, SPS bears the burden to show that the proposed

  increase is just and reasonable. 4 A stipulated resolution remains subject to the Commission’s

     independent review. The focus in evaluating any Stipulation of a Future Test Year rate case is on

 the conditions when rates take effect, not the amount of the negotiated decrease from SPS’s original

 request. Section 62-6-14(D) makes clear the Commission’s statutory obligation:

            The commission shall set rates based on a test period that the commission
            determines best reflects the conditions to be experienced during the period when
            the rates determined by the commission take effect. If a future test period is

Admittedly, Section 62-6-14(D) does not require the applicant to continuously update every future-

test-year assumption. However, “in every application for an increase in rates, it is the utility’s

affirmative burden of proof to show that the increased rate or charge is just and reasonable…” 5

Therefore, when the applicant is aware that material forecast inputs have changed but does not

update its filed future-test-year models, 6 it fundamentally denies the Commission an adequate

basis to find the proposed test year best reflects conditions when conditions take effect, and that

the resulting rates are just and reasonable. The record shows SPS failed to meet this obligation.

A. The Record Shows That Material Resource-Adequacy and Load Inputs Have Become
   Stale

        The evidence concerning SPS’s resource-adequacy forecast is a concrete example of SPS’s

failure to update its forecast. In its Application, SPS claimed a 77-MW capacity shortfall for the

2026–2027 period. 7 However, on cross-examination, SPS witness Justin Gable testified that figure

changed, stating that SPS had already secured a short-term capacity purchase for that period. 8 Mr.

Gable further testified that outages, resource unavailability, and updated load forecasts can affect

SPS’s resource-adequacy calculations and that SPS “make[s] efforts” to keep those resource-

adequacy numbers current. 9. He nevertheless confirmed that the 77-MW shortfall originally

sponsored in his testimony had changed. 10 Indeed, Mr. Gable acknowledged that even the then

B. The ELI Regulatory Asset Illustrates the Stipulation’s Failure to Use Current Data

            SPS initially proposed recovery of an approximately $28 million New Mexico retail ELI

regulatory asset, amortized over two years. 16 As Staff Witness Mauldin explained, SPS’s later

discovery responses, however, supported an updated ELI regulatory-asset balance of

approximately $26 million. 17 Staff accordingly recommended the updated approximately

$26 million balance and a four-year amortization period, producing approximately $6.6 million in

annual amortization expense. 18 The Stipulation extends the amortization period to three years, but

it does not specify or reduce the underlying ELI regulatory-asset balance. 19 While the absence of

that specific number does prove the Stipulation uses SPS’s initially proposed $28 million balance,

it does show that the proponents have not demonstrated they used updated data provided through

discovery. 20 As Mr. Mauldin testified, that the use of the initially proposed ELI balance rather

than the updated amount, would embed approximately $2 million in overstated costs in customer

rates. 21

   balance incorporated in the stipulated revenue requirement, the New Mexico allocation, the

   amortization period, annual expense, and record support for each input. Without that

   reconciliation, the Commission cannot determine whether the stipulated ELI treatment is

   supported by current and verifiable information.

II.    SPS has not carried its burden to show that the stipulated forecast -based jurisdictional
       allocation is just and reasonable.
                A. Jurisdictional allocators determine the share of common system costs charged
                to New Mexico.

           SPS uses jurisdictional allocation factors to divide the costs of its shared production and

   transmission system among New Mexico retail, Texas retail, and FERC wholesale customers. 22

   The factors allocate common production and transmission rate base, O&M, depreciation, taxes,

   and other costs. 23 Staff’s evidence indicates that base-period allocation inputs were developed

   using load-research-based customer-class load factors applied to monthly kWh, whereas the

  future-test-year model uses a forecasted 8,760-hour model for each customer class. 24 And, as

  shown in the table below, SPS forecasts that New Mexico retail peak load will grow significantly

  faster than Texas’ load between the base period ending June 30, 2025, and the projected FTY

  ending November 30, 2027.

        SPS’s use of a forecasted New Mexico allocation factor is not unlawful merely because

Texas employs a different test-period framework. The relevant question is whether SPS has

demonstrated that the factor used to assign shared production and transmission costs to New

Mexico reasonably reflects New Mexico’s responsibility for those costs during the rate-effective

period. NMSA 1978, §§ 62-6-14(D), 62-8-7(A).

        Staff’s concern is that the record does not provide a transparent reconciliation between the

forecasted New Mexico allocation factors used in this case and the treatment of the same shared-

system cost pools in the other relevant jurisdictional contexts. 25 Without that reconciliation, the

Commission cannot determine whether the forecasted New Mexico factor is consistently applied

             Blank Direct Testimony at 8–10, 14

 to a defined common-cost universe, whether the remaining shares are calculated on a comparable

basis, or whether the resulting allocation assigns New Mexico an unsupported portion of shared

costs.

         Staff asks the Commission to require SPS to carry its burden of proving that the New

Mexico retail allocation of shared costs is supported, verifiable, and just and reasonable under New

Mexico law. While Staff does not content that the differences between New Mexico and Texas

rates are per se discriminatory, these facts do demonstrate the importance of ensuring the allocation

of common system costs to New Mexico rests on a coherent and verifiable methodology.

B. The mismatch creates the risk of recovery above 100% of the shared cost pool.

         For any common SPS cost pool, the allocation shares assigned to New Mexico, Texas, and

wholesale customers must collectively equal 100%. A common production, transmission, or

energy cost should only be allocated once among the three jurisdictions. However, because SPS’s

Texas and FERC jurisdictions use historic data to develop allocation factors while New Mexico

uses a forecasted data, it creates an inconsistency, or mismatch, in methodologies. As Dr. Blank

explained, where New Mexico’s forecasted growth materially exceeds Texas’s forecasted growth,

the New Mexico cost-of-service study uses a higher New Mexico share than the share than would

be applied in the Texas proceeding. 26 The resulting mismatch creates a demonstrated risk that

portions of common revenue requirement will be assigned to, and recovered from, New Mexico

customers at an inflated level based upon forecasts that never materialize.




         26
              Blank Direct Test. at 9:10–15.

Staff’s Post-Hearing Brief
         Specifically, the mismatch in cost allocating methods makes it possible for SPS to allocate

costs to New Mexico using the inflated 49.56% forecasted allocator while also using historical

actuals of 55.46% in Texas for allocating system capacity. This asymmetry provides SPS the

opportunity to allocate 105.02% of its integrated-system capacity costs between the two states,

which in turn would allow an unlawful double-recovery at the direct expense of captive New

Mexico ratepayers. 27

        Staff does not need to establish that SPS has already obtained a specific 105% recovery in

a completed Texas rate case to identify the defect. SPS bears the burden of proof, not Staff. The

record establishes that SPS’s proposed method permits New Mexico to be charged using a higher

forecasted allocator without showing that Texas and wholesale shares will be correspondingly

recalculated under the same methodology. Because the Stipulation preserves forecast-based

allocators that materially increase New Mexico’s share of common costs without a consistent,

verifiable basis across jurisdictions, the Commission should reject it rather than approve rates that

discriminate against New Mexico customers.

C.   The mismatch creates an unmitigated risk for New Mexico customers.

        Unlike variable fuel and purchased power adjustments, New Mexico base rates are

established without a custom true-up or refund mechanism. Once rates are set using the forecasted

49.56% allocator, New Mexico retail customers remain locked into paying those inflated capacity

charges even if the projected load growth fails to materialize. Relying on this allocation results in

arbitrary and discriminatory rates between SPS’s Texas and New Mexico customers. As

 Commissioner O’Connell inquired at the public hearing, why should customers in Roswell and

Amarillo pay different rates for service from the same utility? The answer is clear: ideally, they

should not because SPS operates one integrated electric system.

        SPS argues that retail ratemaking remains state-specific, but New Mexico law requires a

fair, just and reasonable end-result, and Commissioner O’Connell’s questions demonstrates an

unfairness that the Commission is required to reject. This is true, even though the NMPRC sets

New Mexico retail rates under New Mexico law, and the Public Utility Commission of Texas sets

Texas retail rates under Texas law. Fairness governs both jurisdictions, contrary to SPS’s assertions

that no ratemaking principle applies to both jurisdictions. 28 Further, applying New Mexico law to

this rate case, Section 62-8-6 prohibits a utility from establishing or maintaining “any unreasonable

differences as to rates of service either as between localities or as between classes of service.”

Here, the Stipulation’s rates, if accepted, would be discriminatory to New Mexico customers who

would more for electricity than Texas customers in the same rate class.              That is per-se

discriminatory and should not be approved by the NMPRC. This is true especially where the

discriminatory rates are based upon stale data showing an extreme disparity in load growth

between its Texas and New Mexico retail jurisdictions.

        SPS misinterprets Dr. Blank’s explanation of the mismatch at issue. The primary issue that

Dr. Blank illustrates is based upon SPS’s witness Hurts testimony that SPS’s FTY Application uses

forecasted energy, production 12-CP, and transmission 12-CP allocators to allocate common

production and transmission rate base, O&M, depreciation, taxes, and other costs among New

unprecedented degree of growth in its New Mexico jurisdiction, with 524 MW of production-

demand growth versus 174 MW in Texas, and 569 of transmission demand growth versus 203 MW

in Texas. 30 The end result is that the Application and resulting Stipulation are not fair, just and

reasonable and, in accordance with Section 62-6-14(D) the Commission “shall direct the utility to

file new rates…”

        If after a hearing the commission finds the proposed rates to be unjust, unreasonable
        or in any way in violation of law, the commission shall determine the just and
        reasonable rates to be charged or applied by the utility for the service in question
        and shall fix the rates by order to be served upon the utility or the commission by
        its order shall direct the utility to file new rates respecting such service that are
        designed to produce annual revenues no greater than those determined by the
        commission in its order to be just and reasonable. Those rates shall thereafter be
        observed until changed, as provided by the Public Utility Act [Chapter 62, Articles
        1 to 6 and 8 to 13 NMSA 1978].

        The Commission’s FTY rule likewise permits the FTY to be established through

adjustments, forecasts, budgets, or other reasonable methods and based upon verifiable, actual

data. 31 Reading these provisions together, the law authorizes—but do not compel—the

Commission to accept every projected input advanced by the utility. The statutory phrase “best

reflects” in Section 62-6-14 imposes a duty upon the Commission to compare and decide if the

FTY rates best reflect the conditions at the time the rates will go into effect. This law is a consumer

protection mechanism that the Commission is required to apply to any FTY application. Other

consumer protection mechanisms have been imposed upon the utility by Commission FTY Rule

       •   FTY costs that are adequately supported by verifiable, known, measurable, or reliably

           forecast conditions; and

       •   a forecasted interjurisdictional allocation factor that materially changes New Mexico’s

           system-cost responsibility but rests on uncertain load, coincident-demand, wholesale-load,

           or loss-factor assumptions.

           Nothing in the FTY statute requires the Commission to accept a forecasted allocator merely

   because it uses FTY costs elsewhere in the cost-of-service model. 33

III.   The Matching Principle is an accounting ratemaking principle that does not override the
       Commission’s statutory duty that the end result of a rate case is to set fair, just and
       reasonable rates.
           SPS argues the Commission should disregard Dr. Blank’s calculation that the revenue

   deficiency was $47 million and not $172 million because its allegedly creates a violation of the

   “matching principle”. However, the Commission should disregard this argument because the

   matching principle is an accounting principle, not a rule of law and most importantly, Commission

   precedent holds that the matching principle is not absolute and does not supersede the

   Commission’s duty to ensure the end result of a rate case is fair, just and reasonable rates. 34

           Case No. 12-00007-UT expressly ruled that matching principle must give way to achieve

   fair, just and reasonable rates, stating that: “Allowing PNM to recover costs of the SPS and Tri-

        Here, the Commission should adopt Dr. Blank’s adjustment of the jurisdictional allocation

ratio and rule that a lack of complete synchronization is acceptable to achieve fair, just and

A. Broad Support from parties representing special interests cannot substitute for

attached to its Statement in Opposition to the Stipulation 36, Staff did not oppose every Section in

the Stipulation and very selectively decided which Sections were in the public interest and which

were not. Staff’s Post Hearing Brief, while still recommending the Commission adopt its Direct

        SPS misstates Staff requests, because Staff is not asking the asking the Commission to

impose a rewritten agreement on unwilling parties; rather, the Commission may deny the proposed

Stipulation while leaving the Signatories free either proceed to a public hearing on the merits of

the Application as filed, or to decide if they wish to pursue a revised resolution consistent with the

evidence and the Commission’s public-interest obligations as demonstrated by Exhibit A.II

attached to Staff’s Post Hearing Brief. Contrary to statement of SPS on page 1, as a whole, the

Stipulation does not benefit the public interest; does not result in fair just and reasonable rates and

is not fair to NM residential customers to be allocated a higher percentage of the rate increases

than large customers and to pay more for the exact same Kwh than Texas customers in the same

class. Staff is obligated to oppose a unreasonable Stipulation built on a faulty foundation of stale,

not updated forecasted data that hasn't been updated for known and measurable changes during the

linkage period.

        Staff did not and is not advocating for the Commission to re-write the Stipulation. Rather,

Staff has consistently requested that the Commission to reject the Stipulation, and only as an

alternative, that the Commission could impose conditions of approval, for the Signatories to accept

or reject, and if reject, then proceed to a public hearing on the Application. SPS suggests that the

Commission must accept the Stipulation since the intervenors signed. The number of signatories

is determinative to the issue of approval of a stipulation. The public interest is determinative. In

this case, SPS didn’t receive Staff’s approval and Staff is the most important because Staff is the

only party that represents the public interest and not a special interest. The intervenors are bound

  therefore should due consideration to Staff more than the other parties. Contrary to SPS’s

IV.   The Cunningham BESS and PTC provisions require enforceable, verifiable benefit-
      allocation protections
          SPS’s Post Hearing Brief essentially re-writes the Stipulation to add words that are not

  there. SPS states: 37

          The Stipulation directly assigns all Cunningham BESS costs to New Mexico because New
          Mexico customers will receive the associated capacity, energy-arbitrage, and ancillary-
          service benefits. That is, when allocating shared production-capacity costs between New
          Mexico and Texas, SPS adjusts the 12-CP allocator to credit New Mexico with the capacity
          Cunningham provides to serve New Mexico peak load. That adjustment reduces New
          Mexico’s share of shared production capacity costs. SPS also credits New Mexico
          customers with Cunningham’s net energy arbitrage and ancillary-service value, as
          measured by Southwest Power Pool market settlements, through SPS’s FPPCAC. In short,
          the Stipulation uses Cunningham’s capacity benefit to reduce New Mexico’s allocated
          production-capacity costs and its market benefits to reduce FPPCAC costs.

          Staff does not take issue with this explanation. However, this is the first time that Staff has

  seen it in writing, and it is explicitly stated in the Stipulation; and therefore, it is not binding on

  SPS; or enforceable by the Signatories. Accordingly, there is no provision that ensures New

  Mexico customers will receive 100% of the benefits they paid for.

          This is particularly concerning given SPS’s less than fulsome commitment to New Mexico

  customers’ benefits when it states 38: “The ACAP/PRM formula reasonably measures the New

  Mexico load Cunningham can serve. The remaining dispute concerns how much New Mexico peak

 load Cunningham’s accredited capacity can reliably support.” That is not the remaining dispute.

Rather, the remaining dispute is whether SPS will commit to the principle that when New Mexico

customers pay 100% for a resource, then New Mexico customers should receive 100% of the

energy and capacity benefits.

        Staff’s concern is that the Stipulation does not have a specific, enforceable, auditable

mechanism for ensuring that New Mexico receives the complete economic capacity value

attributable to a resource for which New Mexico customers are assigned the full cost. Staff

maintains its position that New Mexico should receive the full-ACAP of Cunningham. Staff is not

asking for more than 100% of the benefits. SPS’s use of its “peak load adjustment” is unfair to

New Mexicans and should be disregarded by the Commission 39 because, Staff’s full-ACAP

approach does not give New Mexico too large a credit to New Mexico customers. Staff’s proposal

to subtract Cunningham’s entire accredited capacity from New Mexico’s peak load, is fair, just and

reasonable because it results in New Mexico customers receiving 100% of the 24 MW of

accredited capacity without regard to whether or not it could serve 24 MW of peak load.

A. The Commission Should Reject the Stipulation’s PRM Adjustment for Cunningham
